KEYWORDS: Human adenovirus type 7, case fatality rate, phylogenetic analysis, global epidemiology, acute respiratory disease status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2025 Jul 9; Accepted 2025 Oct 28; Collection date 2025. Introduction Human adenovirus (HAdV) is a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA virus with a genome of up to 35 kb, classified into seven species (A-G) based on serology, gene homology, and whole-genome sequences. Currently, 116 genotypes have been reported, evaluated, and cataloged ( http://hadvwg.gmu.edu/ ). While most HAdV infections are self-limiting, severe or fatal outcomes, such as respiratory failure, can occur in infants, immunocompromised individuals, and children.[ 1–3 ]. HAdV-7, a highly prevalent type of HAdV-B, is associated with hyperinflammatory syndrome and severe clinical outcomes, particularly in children and military recruits, with the highest recorded case fatality rate (CFR) at 31.1% [ 4 ]. Children infected with HAdV-7 often experience prolonged fever, tachypnea, dyspnea, and are at a higher risk of fatality [ 4–10 ]. Outbreaks have also been reported among U.S. college students and military recruits, with over 10,000 cases of HAdV-7/−4 annually since 1999, attributed to depleted vaccine stocks [ 11 , 12 ]. Globally, HAdV-7 accounts for approximately 20% of respiratory adenovirus infections [ 13 , 14 ]. Since 1978, HAdV-7 has been classified into at least 19 genotypes, with HAdV-7b being dominant in China before 1980, followed by HAdV-7d from 1980 to 1990 [ 15–17 ]. Recently, the re-emergence of HAdV-7d has been linked to severe disease [ 18 , 19 ]. This report discusses the global prevalence, clinical characteristics, and phylogenomics of HAdV-7 over the past 70 years since its initial identification, offering insights for its prevention, control, and vaccine development. Methods Electronic literature search and article selection for HAdV-7 A systematic search for peer-reviewed articles was conducted in PubMed to identify relevant publications based on the search strategy “((((“Adenovirus”[Text Word] OR “adenoviruses”[Text Word] OR “adenoviral”[Text Word] OR “mastadenovirus*”[Text Word] OR “AdV”[Text Word] OR “HAdV”[Text Word]) AND (“type 7”[Text Word] OR “types 7”[Text Word] OR “subtype 7”[Text Word] OR “subtypes 7”[Text Word] OR “serotype 7”[Text Word] OR “serotypes 7”[Text Word] OR “genotype 7”[Text Word] OR “genotypes 7”[Text Word] OR “HAdV-B7”[Text Word] OR “HAdV-7”[Text Word] OR “HAdV7”[Text Word] OR “Ad7”[Text Word] OR “Ad-7”[Text Word] OR “Adv7"[Text Word] OR “Adv-7”[Text Word]) AND 1954/01/01:2023/12/31[Date – Publication]) NOT “Fowl"[All Fields]”. The titles, abstracts, and full texts of the articles were independently evaluated against the eligibility criteria by two reviewers. Articles were included in the meta-analysis if they satisfied the following criteria: (1) the adenovirus“type/serotype/subtype/genotype” is mentioned in the abstract or keywords, including abbreviations (e.g. HAdV, HAdV-B7, Adv, Ad, etc.), and (2) original/primary evidence for the detection of HAdV-7 is reported in surveillance or epidemiological studies, case reports, or laboratory/bioinformatics studies involving human clinical samples or data derived from human clinical samples. The following studies were excluded: (1) the adenovirus “type/serotype/subtype/genotype” or abbreviation was not mentioned in the abstract; (2) the article was published prior to January 1954 or after December 2023; (3) reliable serotyping and genotyping methods for identifying HAdV-7 from clinical samples were not employed; (4) original/primary evidence for HAdV-7 detection was not reported. All data initially identified as HAdV-7 h (later reclassified as HAdV-B66) [ 20 ] were manually excluded during the collection process. Refer to Supplementary Table 4 for a list of included studies. Data extraction and statistical analysis Relevant data (e.g. HAdV-7 infections, location, disease characteristics, and patient demographics) were extracted from full-text articles utilizing a specifically designed data collection form, along with visual data analysis conducted using GraphPad Prism 8.0. Rapid electronic literature search and article selection for fatal HAdV genotypes To investigate the distribution of HAdV genotypes in fatal cases, a rapid literature search was conducted in PubMed using the search strategy “((“Adenovirus”[Title/Abstract] OR “Adenoviruses”[Title/Abstract] OR “Adenoviral”[Title/Abstract] OR “Adenoviridae”[Mesh])) AND ((“death”[Title/Abstract] OR “died”[Title/Abstract] OR “deceased”[Title/Abstract] OR “mortality”[Title/Abstract] OR “fatality”[Title/Abstract] OR “fatal”[Title/Abstract] OR “lethal”[Title/Abstract] OR “deadly”[Title/Abstract] OR “Mortality”[Mesh] OR “Fatal Outcome”[Mesh]))”. Article types such as Autobiography, Bibliography, Biography, Books and Documents, Comment, Editorial, Interview, Retracted Publication, Review, and Systematic Review were excluded. Phylogenetic analyses of HAdV-7 penton base, hexon, fibre, and whole genome sequences and amino acid mutation analyses of the three capsid proteins We utilized the NCBI keywords “human adenovirus 7” and “human adenovirus P7H7F7,” setting the sequence length to 30,000–40,000 bp. A total of 315 HAdV-7 whole genome sequences were retrieved. Among these, the fibre gene sequences of two isolates ( MH910665.1 from 1998 and JX423386.1 from 2003) exhibited a high identity of 99.8% with the counterpart from HAdV-3, while their identity with the remaining HAdV-7 isolates was considerably lower at 63.59%. According to the latest genotyping criteria, these two isolates belong to the HAdV-B66 type, which is recombinant (previously designated as HAdV-7 h) [ 20 ]. These two isolates significantly influenced the construction of the phylogenetic tree for the other isolates and were subsequently excluded, resulting in 313 isolates for analyses. Multiple sequence alignment was performed using MAFFT software [ 21 ], and the NJ phylogenetic trees were constructed with MEGA software [ 22 ], based on the penton base, hexon, fibre, and whole genome sequences of HAdV-7. BioEdit v7.7.1 software was used for amino acid mutation analyses and visualization. Details of the isolates are provided in Supplementary Table 5 . Temporal evolutionary dynamics of HAdV-7 The 313 HAdV-7 whole genome sequences retrieved from GenBank for phylogenetic analysis were further screened for collection dates. Entries lacking collection dates were excluded, yielding a total of 286 HAdV-7 genome sequences for temporal evolutionary dynamics analysis. The most suitable substitution model for the nucleotide sequence matrix of the HAdV-7 whole genome was identified as GTR + I + G4, based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) using ModelTest-ng v0.1.7 software [ 23 ]. Whole genome sequences of HAdV-7 were analyzed using BEAST v1.10.4 software [ 24 ], which enabled the calculation of the evolutionary rate of nucleotides and the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) among each variant. An uncorrelated relaxed lognormal molecular clock model combined with the population exponential growth model was employed to run 5 × 10 8 –6 × 10 8 generations six times, with sampling every 1,000 generations and data integration through LogCombiner. The data generated from Beast sampling were subsequently analyzed using Tracer v1.7.2 software, ensuring that all model parameters had an effective sample size (ESS) greater than 200 and a burn-in percentage of 10%. Additionally, the maximum clade credibility (MCC) tree was estimated using the posterior probability method, and the evolutionary tree was constructed and analyzed using FigTree v1.4.4 software. Results Article screening and geographical distribution of HAdV-7 Reports We conducted a systematic search of the PubMed database utilizing specific keywords, resulting in the identification of 726 publications. Of these, 430 articles were excluded from the study due to the absence of information regarding the “type/serotype/subtype/genotype” of adenovirus in their abstracts and keywords. A comprehensive analysis of the full texts of the remaining 324 articles (including twenty-eight manually searched) was performed, leading to the selection of 305 articles for inclusion in this qualitative review. Out of these, 301 articles met the criteria for the quantitative review ( Figure 1 , Supplementary Table 4 ). Figure 1. PRISMA flow diagram illustrating the identification, screening, and review of the medical and scientific literature on HAdV-7 infections, published from 1954 to 2023. The search strategy on PubMed was “((((“Adenovirus”[Text Word] OR “adenoviruses”[Text Word] OR “adenoviral”[Text Word] OR “mastadenovirus*”[Text Word] OR “AdV”[Text Word] OR “HAdV”[Text Word]) AND (“type 7”[Text Word] OR “types 7”[Text Word] OR “subtype 7”[Text Word] OR “subtypes 7”[Text Word] OR “serotype 7”[Text Word] OR “serotypes 7”[Text Word] OR “genotype 7”[Text Word] OR “genotypes 7”[Text Word] OR “HAdV-B7”[Text Word] OR “HAdV-7”[Text Word] OR “HAdV7”[Text Word] OR “Ad7”[Text Word] OR “Ad-7”[Text Word] OR “Adv7”[Text Word] OR “Adv-7”[Text Word]) AND 1954/01/01:2023/12/31[Date – Publication]) NOT “Fowl"[All Fields]”, which retrieved a total of 726 articles. Reports on HAdV-7 infections have emerged from all continents except Antarctica. Specifically, 173 articles (56.72%) were published from Asia, 60 from North America (19.67%), 41 from Europe (13.44%), 16 from South America (5.25%), nine from Africa (2.95%), and six from Oceania (1.97%). China (encompassing Hong Kong and Taiwan) contributed the largest number of articles, totalling 113 (37.05%), followed by the United States with 56 (18.36%), Japan with 20 (6.56%), and the United Kingdom with 16 (5.25%). In total, 301 articles documented specific cases of HAdV-7 infections, amounting to 16,100 cases and 388 associated deaths (CFR: 2.41%), which were subsequently included in our quantitative review detailing the global distribution of HAdV-7 infections. The reported number of HAdV-7 infections per article varied from 1 to 1,034. Time distribution of HAdV-7 infections The annual publication rate of articles reporting HAdV-7 infections has shown a notable increase over time, with 122 articles (40.00%) published in the last decade ( Figure 2 ), including 82 from China (encompassing Hong Kong and Taiwan). Figure 2. Number of peer-reviewed publications documenting HAdV-7 infections in the medical and scientific literature by decade from 1954 to 2023. Yearly reported HAdV-7 infections have also risen consistently, with military students and personnel accounting for 2,999 cases over the past ten years, representing 58.23% of the total military infections. Furthermore, the number of reported HAdV-7 infections in the decade following 2014 (9,044 cases) was 3.4 times greater than in the preceding decade (2,630 cases) ( Figure 3 a). It is important to note that the year of publication may not accurately reflect the year in which the reported HAdV-7 infections occurred; data for specific years included in each study are detailed in Supplementary Table 4 . Figure 3. (a). Reported cases of military and civilian HAdV-7 infections in the medical and scientific literature, 1954–2023. The decade of publication may not accurately represent the decade in which each reported HAdV-7 infection occurred. (b). Reported cases of HAdV-7 infections in the medical and scientific literature, categorized by geographic region, 1954–2023. (c). Reported fatal cases related to HAdV-7 infections in the medical and scientific literature, categorized by geographic region, 1954-2023. Total deaths reported across each continent are indicated in black; deaths reported by countries/regions with at least 9 reported cases are displayed in various colours. Geographic distribution of HAdV-7 infections The majority of reported HAdV-7 infections were found in Asia, totalling 10,827 cases (67.25%), followed by North America with 3,397 cases (21.10%), Europe with 958 cases (5.95%), South America with 633 cases (3.93%), Africa with 172 cases (1.07%), and Oceania with 113 cases (0.70%). Most fatalities occurred in Asia, totalling 249 cases (64.18%), followed by North America with 57 cases (14.69%). In Asia, Mainland China reported the highest number of HAdV-7 infections, accounting for 7,861 cases (72.61%), followed by Japan (997 cases, 9.21%), South Korea (843 cases, 7.79%), and Singapore (465 cases, 4.29%), with Taiwan reporting 342 cases (3.16%). In North America, 99.00% of the 3,397 cases were from the United States (3,363 cases), with the remainder from Canada (34 cases, 1.00%). Of the 958 cases reported in Europe, 55.53% were from the United Kingdom (532 cases), 24.43% from Finland (234 cases), 7.10% from the Netherlands (68 cases), 5.22% from Sweden (50 cases), and 3.03% from Norway (29 cases). South America reported a total of 633 HAdV-7 infections, distributed as follows: Argentina (351 cases, 55.45%), Chile (170 cases, 26.86%), Brazil (77 cases, 12.16%), Uruguay (8 cases, 1.26%), Colombia (4 cases, 0.63%) and other regions (23 cases, 3.63%) include aggregated data from Chile, Uruguay, Argentina, Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia. In Africa, 64.53% of the 172 reported cases were from South Africa (111 cases), followed by Egypt (43 cases, 25.00%), with 9.88% from Bantu children (no specific country) (17 cases), and 0.58% from Tunisia (1 cases). Oceania reported cases from two countries: Australia with 108 cases and New Zealand with 5 cases, representing 95.58% and 4.42%, respectively. Civilians and military personnel/students accounted for 67.95% (10,940 cases) and 31.99% (5,150 cases) of all infections, respectively ( Table 1 , Figure 3 a). The majority of civilian infections were reported in Asia, while military infections were primarily documented in North America (2,533 cases) and Asia (2,389 cases). Demographic distribution and diseases related to HAdV-7 infections Among 16,100 patients with HAdV-7 infection, 14,688 were categorized by age. Of these, 8,336 (56.75%) were children (under 18 years old) and 6,352 (43.25%) were adults (≥18 years old). Among the adult patients, 5,150 (81.08%) were military students or personnel, indicating a high susceptibility to clustered outbreaks of HAdV-7 in military settings. After excluding military personnel, only 1,092 adult cases remained, suggesting that children are the main susceptible population in the general community. Gender distribution analysis showed that among 5,880 patients with gender information, 4,484 (76.26%) were male and 1,396 (23.74%) were female, indicating a higher susceptibility to HAdV-7 in males. Among the articles meeting the inclusion criteria, 278 reported clinical symptoms in patients with HAdV-7 infections. Respiratory symptoms were the most frequently identified ( Table 1 ). Among patients with HAdV-7 infection, 11,617 cases (72.16%) involved respiratory infections, including pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections, acute laryngotracheal infections, acute laryngotracheobronchitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), pharyngobronchitis, and pleuropneumonia. Additionally, gastrointestinal infections were documented in 957 cases (5.94%), while ocular infections were reported in 456 cases (2.83%), commonly presenting with symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea, and conjunctival congestion. Notably, 126 cases of HAdV-7 infection were accompanied by encephalitis-related symptoms. Deaths caused by HAdV-7 infections Among all infected patients, 6,183 (38.40%) required hospitalization, highlighting the considerable severity associated with HAdV-7 infection. Among those hospitalized, 5,795 survived, with a median hospitalization of 9 days (ranging from 1 to 240 days). In contrast, 388 patients died, accounting for 6.28% of all hospitalized cases, with a median hospitalization of 10 days (range: 1–79 days). Detailed data are provided in Table 1 . Among the 388 deaths associated with HAdV-7 infection, 87.63% (340/388) occurred in children while 8.76% (34/388) in adults. The leading three countries in reported fatalities were Mainland China (150 cases), the United States (53 cases), and South Korea (39 cases). Other regions with at least nine reported deaths included Argentina (23 cases), Taiwan (15 cases), Japan (12 cases), Bantu children (11 cases), the United Kingdom (9 cases), Russia (9 cases) and Singapore (9 cases) ( Figure 3 c). Asia accounted for 249 deaths, while North America reported 57 deaths; Europe, South America, Africa, and Oceania reported 29, 25, 17, and 11 deaths, respectively. In Asia, a study from Guangzhou China (2010–2021) recorded the highest number of deaths (27 cases) among children with HAdV-7-related bronchiolitis obliterans and bronchiectasis, with 2 cases confirmed as genotype HAdV-7d [ 25 ]. Another study (2018–2020) documented 14 pediatric deaths, including cases complicated by viral encephalitis, with 3 isolated strains identified as genotype HAdV-7d [ 4 ]. In Taiwan, an outbreak from 2010–2011 resulted in 7 HAdV-7 pediatric fatalities among 45 severe cases in children [ 3 ]. South Korea reported 11 pediatric deaths from HAdV-7 infections (1995–2004), with 10 cases attributed to HAdV-7d and one to HAdV-7 l. [ 26 ], while Japan recorded five infant deaths due to HAdV-7 during a 1995 outbreak, one of which was identified as HAdV-7d2. [ 27 ]. In the Philippines, severe malnutrition and high fever were linked to 6 HAdV-7 deaths in children aged 2–59 months [ 28 ]. In North America, a 1998 outbreak in Chicago resulted in 8 deaths among 31 pediatric cases due to HAdV-7d2 infections, marking a significant outbreak in the U.S. [ 29 ]. In Europe, a UK-based study reported fatal HAdV-7 infections in an immunocompetent adult with respiratory failure [ 30 ], indicating the potential for HAdV-7 to cause severe lower respiratory tract infections in adults. In Africa, a HAdV-7 outbreak among Bantu children in South Africa in 1967 caused 11 fatalities, with serological confirmation as HAdV-7a. Notably, nine patients presented neurological manifestations, particularly encephalitis, which became a defining characteristic of this epidemic [ 31 ]. In South America, in a study conducted in Argentina by P.R. Barrero et al. [ 32 ] (1999–2000) on patients with adenovirus-associated acute lower respiratory infections, HAdV-7 was responsible for 19 fatalities. Among these, 14 cases were mono-infections and 5 were co-infections (four with HAdV-1 and one with HAdV-2). Notably, HAdV-7 exhibited the highest detection rate (63.64%, 14/22) among all fatal mono-adenoviral infections. Similarly, in Oceania, five children in Auckland (1959–1963) died from HAdV-7-related respiratory infections, with some presenting with diarrhea [ 33 ]. These findings underscore the global impact of HAdV-7, particularly in Asia, and its association with severe outcomes, including encephalitis and respiratory failure. HAdV-7: the most prevalent genotype associated with fatalities To our knowledge, a total of 200 articles reporting fatal HAdV infections were identified, involving 6 HAdV species (A-F) and 29 types, which encompassed 667 fatal cases ( Figure 4 ). Among these, infections caused by HAdV-B accounted for the highest proportion (65.74%), with HAdV-7 being the most prevalent type, responsible for 262 fatalities (39.28%). HAdV-C accounted for the second largest proportion of fatalities (22.95%), of which HAdV-C2 was responsible for 9.78%. However, severe outcomes associated with HAdV-C infection predominantly occurred in patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell or solid organ transplantation [ 34–36 ]. The remaining four HAdV species (A, D, E, F) each accounted for less than 5% of fatal cases (4.19%, 2.02%, 3.30%, and 1.80%, respectively). Accordingly, these findings indicate that HAdV-7 is the most prevalent genotype linked to fatal outcomes. Figure 4. Phylogenetic analyses identified four lineages and the currently prevalent 7E2 variant associated with more fatalities A phylogenetic tree derived from HAdV-7 whole genome sequences revealed four distinct lineages ( Figure 5 ). Lineage 1 (Red) included the HAdV-7 prototype strain ( AY594255.1 , identified in 1954) first reported in the U.S., along with isolates gz07 ( HQ659699.1 , from 2007) and GZ08 ( GQ478341.1 , from 2008) from China. Lineage 2 (Green) comprised three vaccine strains from China and the U.S. ( AY495969.1 ; AY594256.1 ; MN936178.1 , from 2008) and five additional isolates, collectively termed the HAdV-7 V variant. The remaining closely related sequences formed the HAdV-7E variant, which was further divided into the early prevalent lineage 3 (Blue) and the continuously prevalent lineage 4 (Purple). Lineage 3 (Blue) was smaller, containing only a few early isolates (1988–1999) from the United States, such as CL_44 ( KF268125.1 , from 1988, genotype 7a) and ak40 ( JX423388.1 , from 1997, genotype 7b) designated as the HAdV-7E1 variant. Lineage 4 (Purple) encompassed all remaining isolates, nearly 300 sequences, including isolate ak35 ( JX423383.1 , from 2006, genotype 7d) and the recently uploaded isolate 8037 ( OR487156.1 , from 2023), which we designated the HAdV-7E2 variant. The phylogenetic tree was constructed using the neighbor-joining method based on the Kimura two-parameter model with 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Lineage 1 (red): HAdV-7p prototype strains and early Chinese isolates; Lineage 2 (green): HAdV-7 V vaccine strains and closely related isolates; Lineage 3 (blue): Early HAdV-7E1 U.S. variants (1988-1999); Lineage 4 (purple): The predominant contemporary HAdV-7E2 variants (2006-present). Furthermore, we analyzed the genotypes of HAdV-7 strains isolated from fatal cases. In earlier periods, genotyping was primarily performed using restriction enzyme analysis (e.g. 7a, 7b, 7d). Since 2009, however, isolates have been characterized and typed based on whole-genome sequencing [ 37 ]. HAdV-7 strains isolated from fatal cases showed a distinct temporal pattern in genotype distribution ( Supplementary Figure 3 ). Specifically, genotypes such as 7a and 7b were primarily detected in earlier time periods (prior to 1989) and had largely disappeared since 2005. The 7E1 variant (represented by orange-toned bars) according to the whole genomic phylogenetic analysis included early genotypes such as 7a and 7b. In contrast, genotypes 7d and 7d2, which were identified as 7E2 variant (shown in blue-toned bars) according to the whole genomic phylogenetic analysis, have emerged as the dominant circulating strains since 2005. The analysis revealed that the currently prevalent 7E2 variant was associated with more fatalities (91 cases, 67.91%) than the 7E1 variant (43 cases, 32.09%). Our analysis of the genomic average nucleotide identity among different variants ( Supplementary Figure 2 ) revealed high within-group identity, exceeding 99.807%, while substantial divergence was observed between variants. The 7p prototype (lineage 1) exhibited the greatest differences compared to the other three variants (98.127%−98.263%). In contrast, the nucleotide identity among the other three variants remained relatively high, all above 99.500% (ranging from 99.540% to 99.878%). These results suggest that through population dynamics and adaptation, the emerged variants have accumulated significant genetic divergence compared to 7p prototype. Furthermore, we analyzed the nucleotide identity ( Supplementary Figure 3 ) and key amino acid mutation sites ( Supplementary Table 1–3 ) of the three capsid proteins. High within-variant identity was identified (exceeding 99.800%), while notable differences were identified between variants. For the penton base gene, the 7 V variant exhibited relatively low sequence identity (98.070–98.310%) compared to other variants. It contained 7 mutation sites relative to the prototype 7p, and 4–5 mutations when compared to the other two circulating variants. In the hypervariable region (HVR), the 7 V variant carried an I158 T mutation. Within the RGD region, the 7 V variant showed a Q338H mutation, the 7E1 variant exhibited a E320 V mutation, and the majority of 7E2 variants featured a D325N mutation ( Supplementary Table 1) . The hexon gene exhibited the greatest divergence, with identity between the 7p prototype and the other three variants ranging from 97.350% to 97.460%. These differences were primarily localized in HVR1 (7 sites) and HVR7 (12 sites) ( Supplementary Table 2 ). In contrast, the 7 V variant showed high identity (99.730–99.750%) with the other two circulating variants, indicating strong conservation among all currently prevalent HAdV-7 isolates except the three prototype strains. Given that the hexon protein is a major target for neutralizing antibodies, these results suggest that U.S. military HAdV-7 vaccines developed based on the 7 V variant are still functional in protection against the prevalent 7E1 and 7E2 variants. In the case of the fibre protein, the 7p prototype demonstrated considerable divergence from the other three variants (98.710–99.010%), featuring 2–3 mutations in the tail region and 1–3 mutations in the knob domain (Supplementary Table 3) . The differences among the other three variants were less than 0.600%. These findings suggest that currently prevalent HAdV-7 isolates do not exhibit significant fibre diversity. However, certain mutations in the knob coding region between the prototype and circulating isolates – such as T142R (present in 7 V, 7E1, and 7E2 variants), I147 V (found in a subset of 7E2 variant) and I273 T (7E1 variant) – may influence receptor interaction and potentially alter viral adsorption efficiency. Based on amino acid mutation analysis, a number of unique background mutation sites were identified in HAdV-7E1 or HAdV-7E2 variants. This suggests that HAdV-7E1 and HAdV-7E2 variants evolved independently from the prototype strain. Over the course of their circulation, the prevalence of these two variants in the human population has shifted, with HAdV-7E2 currently becoming the predominant variant. Evolutionary divergence times of HAdV-7 Using the Bayesian-MCMC method, we performed a whole-genome analysis of HAdV-7 isolates from five countries – China (200 isolates), the United States (81 isolates), Russia (3 isolates), Japan (1 isolate), and Germany (1 isolate) – to reconstruct the temporal dynamics, estimate the mean nucleotide substitution rate, infer the time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA), and investigate evolutionary divergence. The average nucleotide substitution rate of HAdV-7 was found to be 3.89 × 10 −5 mutations/site/year (95% HPD: 3.05–4.76 × 10 −5 ). The tMRCA was estimated to have occurred in 1821 (95% HPD: 1717-1891), marking the first evolutionary divergence that separated the HAdV-7 prototype from other isolates. The second divergence occurred in 1907 (95% HPD: 1870-1933), resulting in the separation of the HAdV-7 V and HAdV-7E variants. The third divergence emerged in 1978 (95% HPD: 1964-1987), dividing the HAdV-7E variant into the HAdV-7E1 and HAdV-7E2 variants ( Figure 7 ). The estimated timing of all major divergence events suggests a pattern of periodic emergence. Accordingly, these findings indicate that a new variant of HAdV-7 emerges approximately every 70–80 years. Figure 7. Bayesian estimation of the time to the most recent common ancestor for HAdV-7. The red dots indicate the three major evolutionary divergences among the four subtypes, and the 95% highest posterior density (HPD) range for the time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) is presented. The average nucleotide substitution rate of HAdV-7 was calculated at 3.89 × 10 −5 mutations/site/year (95% HPD: 3.05–4.76 × 10 −5 ). The most recent common ancestor is estimated to have appeared in 1821 (95% HPD: 1717-1891), while the most recent 7E2 variant ancestor emerged in 1978 (95% HPD: 1964–1987). Discussion It has been 70 years since Berge et al. [ 38 ] first identified HAdV-7 in 1954. We conducted a meta-analysis of global HAdV-7 infections from 1954 to 2023, revealing a steady increase in reported cases and literature over time ( Figure 2 ). Notably, 40.00% of reports were published in the last decade, with 66.75% focusing on civilian cases. The incidence of HAdV-7 infections has risen steadily, with military-related infections surging; 58.23% of cases were reported in the past 10 years. Additionally, the number of civilian infections reported in the decade since 2014 was 3.4 times greater than that of the previous decade ( Figure 3 a), indicating that HAdV-7 infections are prevalent in both military and civilian populations and may be on the rise. This phenomenon may be attributed to improved diagnostic capabilities and increased public health awareness. In patients infected with HAdV-7, we observed that children (56.75%) and military personnel (35.06%) constituted the primary susceptible groups, accounting for 91.81% of cases with documented age information. Additionally, the number of male infected individuals (4,484 cases) was 3.21 times higher than that of females (1,396 cases), which aligns with the clinical findings reported by Wei et al. [ 4 , 39 , 40 ], collectively indicating a higher susceptibility to HAdV-7 among males. Furthermore, in a study involving intravenous injection of mice with a high dose of HAdV-5, male mice exhibited more severe pathological damage and significantly higher fatality compared to females [ 41 ]. These results suggest that HAdV infection may lead to more severe clinical outcomes, including a higher risk of fatality, in males. HAdV-7 cases have been reported on all continents except Antarctica, with Asia exhibiting the highest incidence, particularly in Mainland China. This contrasts with the global epidemic trend of HAdV-4 infections between 1960 and 2020, as studied by Coleman et al. [ 42 ]. The majority of HAdV-4 infection cases (21,130 cases, 86.14%) occurred in North America, primarily concentrated in the United States (21,124 cases, 86.12%), while Asia accounted for only 7.05%. Among these, the number of HAdV-4 cases reported in Mainland China was 147, representing just 0.60% of the total infections. This phenomenon is likely attributable to the U.S. military’s vaccination strategy. Routine HAdV-4 and HAdV-7 vaccinations for military recruits, implemented in 1971, drastically reduced infections. However, following their discontinuation in 1997, HAdV-4 resurged, while HAdV-7 infections increased only slightly, [ 12 , 43–45 ]. To our knowledge, no systematic retrospective studies have been conducted on other HAdV types. However, HAdV-3 infections have exhibited varying prevalence rates globally: South Korea (1990–1998, 15%; 1991–2007, 37%; 2010, 74.3%) [ 46–48 ]; Mainland China (1976–1980, 39.08%; 2006–2008, 43.48%; 2009–2012, 37.3%) [ 49–51 ]. These variations underscore the influence of specific HAdV types, vaccination status, and regional factors on infection patterns. Investigating HAdV-specific infections by time and region can help inform vaccine interventions aimed at reducing morbidity and fatality. Different types of HAdV present varying manifestations and severity. Among them, HAdV-7 is highly pathogenic, often resulting in severe outcomes, including death, with the CFR of 2.41%. This rate is significantly higher than that of HAdV-4 (0.11%) [ 42 ]. This suggests that HAdV-7 infections are more severe. Deaths from HAdV-7 have been reported in 26 countries, with encephalitis being a notable complication, as highlighted by Gerber et al [ 29 ]. In contrast, HAdV-4 fatalities were primarily due to respiratory complications, with only one case of encephalitis reported [ 52 ]. We also found that among the distribution of HAdV genotypes associated with fatalities, HAdV-7 accounted for the highest proportion (262 cases, 39.28%). Phylogenetic analysis of 313 HAdV-7 genomes revealed four clusters: HAdV-7 prototype, HAdV-7 V, and HAdV-7E variants, with HAdV-7E further divided into HAdV-7E1 and HAdV-7E2. This classification corresponds approximately with the branches of the whole genome phylogenetic tree previously constructed by Duan et al. [ 53 ]. Based on strains isolated at different times, Duan et al. classified HAdV-7E1 and HAdV-7E2 variants into one cluster. Since 2005, HAdV-7E2 has emerged as the dominant strain globally. Phylogenetic analysis of capsid protein genes indicated that the penton base gene aligns with whole-genome phylogeny, while hexon and fibre genes exhibit distinct clustering patterns. The results of the phylogenetic analysis of a single capsid protein gene are consistent with earlier findings by Li et al. [ 15 , 54–56 ], who classified HAdV-7 into more than 20 genotypes using restriction endonuclease analysis, although this classification did not fully reflect the complete evolutionary characteristics of HAdV-7. For instance, ak38 ( JX423386.1 , from 2003), previously classified as HAdV-7 h, has a higher sequence identity with HAdV-3 and was retyped as HAdV-B66 in 2012 [ 20 ]. Amino acid mutations identified across HAdV-7 variants may alter the spatial conformation of capsid proteins, potentially impacting their biological functions. The knob domain of the adenovirus fibre protein is critical for determining receptor tropism. Notably, the recombinant adenovirus HAdV-D64 acquired its fibre gene from HAdV-D37, which enabled it to infect human corneal epithelial cells and induce significantly stronger corneal inflammation compared to its parental strains [ 57 ]. Species C adenoviruses like HAdV-5 interact with the CAR receptor through apical residues such as Ser408, Pro409, Tyr477 and Leu485 [ 58 ]. HAdV Species B, such as HAdV-7, bind to DSG2 via an extended lateral surface, with key residues including Asn190, Asn192, Asp265, Phe269, and Val300. Mutations at these sites – such as D265A and F269A – have been shown to significantly reduce receptor-binding affinity [ 59 , 60 ]. While HAdV-11 utilizes an “arginine switch” (Arg279-Arg280) for high-affinity binding to CD46, HAdV-7 contains Gln279 at the equivalent position, resulting in only low-affinity, non-functional interaction with CD46 [ 61 ]. In our study, all HAdV-7 strains analyzed retained Gln279 in the fibre knob. However, we identified novel mutations in the knob domain of HAdV-7 variants compared to the HAdV-7p prototype, including T142R (present in HAdV-7 V, 7E1, and 7E2 variants), I147 V (found in some HAdV-7E2 strains), and I273 T (identified in the HAdV-7E1 variant) ( Supplementary Table 3 ). Whether these mutations influence receptor-binding affinity among different HAdV-7 variants requires further investigation. The hypervariable regions (HVRs) of the hexon represent the primary targets of neutralizing antibodies, and their antigenic diversity drives immune evasion [ 62 ]. Intertypic recombination of hexon genes can lead to dramatic antigenic shifts, as seen in the emergence of HAdV-B55 [ 63 ]. Additionally, frequent recombination or point mutations among hexons can result in antigenic drift, exemplified by HAdV-D53 [ 64 ]. Beyond recombination, HVR point mutations can also alter immune recognition via interactions with host factors. For instance, residues in HVR7 of HAdV-5 (I421, T423, E424, T425, and E451) form a binding site for coagulation factor X (FX); FX binding shields neutralizing epitopes and redirects the virus to hepatocytes. Replacing the HVR7 of HAdV-5 with that of HAdV-26, or introducing mutations such as I421G, T423N, E424S, L426Y, and E451Q, completely abolishes the FX-mediated effects in vitro [ 65 ]. In this study, HAdV-7 variants exhibited high similarity among themselves (99.730% to 99.810%), yet showed substantial divergence from the prototype strain (97.350% to 97.460%) ( Supplementary Figure 3 ), with mutations predominantly concentrated in HVR1 and HVR7 (Supplementary Table 2 ). These alterations may disrupt antibody recognition by modifying epitope conformation or mimicking FX-binding mechanisms, thereby enhancing immune evasion and potentially influencing tissue tropism. The penton base mediates virus internalization via its conserved RGD motif, which engages cellular integrins. Karayan et al. demonstrated that not only mutation of the core RGD sequence (R340E) abolished integrin binding and internalization, but substitution of a neighbouring residue (e.g. W165H) also produced a similarly severe defect, indicating that the RGD motif and its surrounding residues form an integrated functional domain [ 66 ]. Notably, Robinson et al. identified a natural penton base recombinant, HAdV-D60, whose penton base gene was derived from HAdV-D37. In HAdV-D60, the RGD loop was deleted and functionally replaced by a Tyr-Gly-Asp (YGD) motif. Peptide inhibition assays confirmed that this YGD motif mediated integrin binding and enhances corneal inflammation [ 67 ]. In our study, we identified several mutations near the RGD motif in HAdV-7 variants, such as Q338H (HAdV-7 V variants), E320 V (HAdV-7E1 variants), and D325N (most strains of HAdV-7E2 variants) ( Table S1 ). Although these do not alter the RGD sequence itself, they may fine-tune integrin-binding efficiency by modulating the local conformation or electrostatic properties of the functional domain, thereby optimizing viral infectivity under immune or tissue-specific selective pressures. The rate of nucleotide substation found for the HAdV-7 genome was 3.89 × 10 −5 mutations/site/year (95% HPD: 3.05-4.76 × 10 −5 ), comparable to the evolutionary rates calculated by Gonzalez Firth, et al. [ 68 , 69 ]: HAdV-E4 (3.24-3.69 × 10 −5 ), HAdV-C (3.46 × 10 −5 ), and HAdV-B (7.20 × 10 −5 ). However, the nucleotide substitution rates of HAdV-7 hexon gene (1.107 × 10 −3 , 95% HPD: 0.541-0.014 × 10 −3 ) and fibre gene (0.132 × 10 −3 , 95% HPD: 0.283-0.014 × 10 −3 ) calculated by Lin et al. are significantly higher for those for nucleotide substation in entire genome [ 70 ]. This discrepancy may be due to a more limited data set, as only 47 HAdV-7 gene sequences were included in the previous study [ 70 ]. Meanwhile, Firth C, et al [ 69 ] revealed that most dsDNA viruses other than adenoviruses – such as HSV-1, VZV, BK virus, and VARV – exhibit nucleotide substitution rates ranging from 6 × 10 − ⁶ to 8 × 10 − ⁵ mutations/site/year. In contrast, as reported by Jenkins GM, et al [ 71 , 72 ], most RNA viruses – including Dengue virus (types 1–4), Human respiratory syncytial virus (A and B), Foot and mouth disease virus (A, C, O), Avian influenza A virus, Human influenza virus (A and C), Hepatitis E virus, and Norovirus – have nucleotide substitution rates between 0.1 × 10 − ³ and 3.8 × 10 − ³ mutations/site/year. This indicates that dsDNA viruses generally undergo mutations at a lower rate during evolution, which is associated with the higher error propensity of RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) compared to DNA polymerase [ 73 ]. Given this pattern, the slow evolutionary rate of HAdV-7 suggests that its genome remains relatively stable over long periods. Our study reveals that it took approximately 70–80 years for HAdV-7 to evolve into a new variant ( Figure 7 ). Therefore, we predict that the next new variant may emerge around the year 2048. Consequently, U.S. military HAdV-7 vaccines developed based on the 7 V variant are still functional in protection against the prevalent 7E1 and 7E2 variants. These findings hold significant implications for future vaccine development. In conclusion, HAdV-7 is a highly pathogenic virus in children with global distribution, particularly in Asia and North America, which together account for 88.35% of the total reported infections, with China and the United States having the highest numbers. Furthermore, HAdV-7 infections were 3.21 times more prevalent in males (4,484 cases) than in females (1,396 cases), indicating a potential higher susceptibility among males. Moreover, HAdV-7 had a higher CFR (2.41%) than HAdV-4 (0.11%) and constituted the most prevalent genotype (39.28%) among fatalities. This significant finding has been largely overlooked. We also described the molecular evolution characteristics of all catalogued HAdV-7 sequences from 1954 to 2023 to provide a foundational reference for HAdV-7 vaccine design and antiviral drug development. However, we acknowledge certain limitations, such as relying on PubMed as the sole source of published articles, thereby excluding medical literature in other languages. Additionally, due to military confidentiality, data regarding infections and deaths within the military may be biased or underreported. Consequently, the number of HAdV-7 infections, deaths, and the CFR reported in our study may be lower than the actual figures. It should be noted that the extent of this reporting discrepancy is also influenced by a country's level of development, healthcare diagnostic capacity, and public health priorities. documents.title: Risk factors for pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: The objective is to systematically gather relevant research to determine and quantify the risk factors and pooled prevalence for pneumonia after a radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer.
METHODS: The reporting procedures of this meta-analysis conformed to the PRISMA 2020. Chinese Wan Fang data, Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Chinese Periodical Full-text Database (VIP), Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, Ovid MEDLINE, PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library from inception to January 20, 2024, were systematically searched for cohort or case-control studies that reported particular risk factors for pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer. The pooled prevalence of pneumonia was estimated alongside risk factor analysis. The quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale after the chosen studies had been screened and the data retrieved. RevMan 5.4 and R 4.4.2 were the program used to perform the meta-analysis.
RESULTS: Our study included data from 20,840 individuals across 27 trials. The pooled prevalence of postoperative pneumonia was 11.0% (95% CI = 8.0% ~ 15.0%). Fifteen risk factors were statistically significant, according to pooled analyses. Several factors were identified to be strong risk factors, including smoking history (OR 2.71, 95% CI = 2.09 ~ 3.50, I2 = 26%), prolonged postoperative nasogastric tube retention (OR 2.25, 95% CI = 1.36-3.72, I2 = 63%), intraoperative bleeding ≥ 200 ml (OR 2.21, 95% CI = 1.15-4.24, I2 = 79%), diabetes mellitus (OR 4.58, 95% CI = 1.84-11.38, I2 = 96%), male gender (OR 3.56, 95% CI = 1.50-8.42, I2 = 0%), total gastrectomy (OR 2.59, 95% CI = 1.83-3.66, I2 = 0%), COPD (OR 4.72, 95% CI = 3.80-5.86, I2 = 0%), impaired respiratory function (OR 2.72, 95% CI = 1.58-4.69, I2 = 92%), D2 lymphadenectomy (OR 4.14, 95% CI = 2.29-7.49, I2 = 0%), perioperative blood transfusion (OR 4.21, 95% CI = 2.51-7.06, I2 = 90%), and hypertension (OR 2.21, 95% CI = 1.29-3.79, I2 = 0%). Moderate risk factors included excessive surgery duration (OR 1.51, 95% CI = 1.25-1.83, I2 = 90%), advanced age (OR 1.91, 95% CI = 1.42-2.58, I2 = 94%), nutritional status (OR 2.62, 95% CI = 1.55-4.44, I2 = 71%), and history of pulmonary disease (OR 1.61, 95% CI = 1.17-2.21, I2 = 79%).
CONCLUSIONS: This study identified 15 independent risk factors significantly associated with pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, with a pooled prevalence of 11.0%. These findings emphasize the importance of targeted preventive strategies, including preoperative smoking cessation, nutritional interventions, blood glucose and blood pressure control, perioperative respiratory training, minimizing nasogastric tube retention time, and optimizing perioperative blood transfusion strategies. For high-risk patients, such as the elderly, those undergoing prolonged surgeries, experiencing excessive intraoperative blood loss, undergoing total gastrectomy, or receiving open surgery, close postoperative monitoring is essential. Early recognition of pneumonia signs and timely intervention can improve patient outcomes and reduce complications.

Abstract Objective The objective is to systematically gather relevant research to determine and quantify the risk factors and pooled prevalence for pneumonia after a radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer. Methods The reporting procedures of this meta-analysis conformed to the PRISMA 2020. Chinese Wan Fang data, Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Chinese Periodical Full-text Database (VIP), Embase, Scopus, CINAHL, Ovid MEDLINE, PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library from inception to January 20, 2024, were systematically searched for cohort or case–control studies that reported particular risk factors for pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer. The pooled prevalence of pneumonia was estimated alongside risk factor analysis. The quality was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale after the chosen studies had been screened and the data retrieved. RevMan 5.4 and R 4.4.2 were the program used to perform the meta-analysis. Results Our study included data from 20,840 individuals across 27 trials. The pooled prevalence of postoperative pneumonia was 11.0% (95% CI = 8.0% ~ 15.0%). Fifteen risk factors were statistically significant, according to pooled analyses. Several factors were identified to be strong risk factors, including smoking history (OR 2.71, 95% CI = 2.09 ~ 3.50, I 2 = 26%), prolonged postoperative nasogastric tube retention (OR 2.25, 95% CI = 1.36–3.72, I 2 = 63%), intraoperative bleeding ≥ 200 ml (OR 2.21, 95% CI = 1.15–4.24, I 2 = 79%), diabetes mellitus (OR 4.58, 95% CI = 1.84–11.38, I 2 = 96%), male gender (OR 3.56, 95% CI = 1.50–8.42, I 2 = 0%), total gastrectomy (OR 2.59, 95% CI = 1.83–3.66, I 2 = 0%), COPD (OR 4.72, 95% CI = 3.80–5.86, I 2 = 0%), impaired respiratory function (OR 2.72, 95% CI = 1.58–4.69, I 2 = 92%), D2 lymphadenectomy (OR 4.14, 95% CI = 2.29–7.49, I 2 = 0%), perioperative blood transfusion (OR 4.21, 95% CI = 2.51–7.06, I 2 = 90%), and hypertension (OR 2.21, 95% CI = 1.29–3.79, I 2 = 0%). Moderate risk factors included excessive surgery duration (OR 1.51, 95% CI = 1.25–1.83, I 2 = 90%), advanced age (OR 1.91, 95% CI = 1.42–2.58, I 2 = 94%), nutritional status (OR 2.62, 95% CI = 1.55–4.44, I 2 = 71%), and history of pulmonary disease (OR 1.61, 95% CI = 1.17–2.21, I 2 = 79%). Conclusions This study identified 15 independent risk factors significantly associated with pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, with a pooled prevalence of 11.0%. These findings emphasize the importance of targeted preventive strategies, including preoperative smoking cessation, nutritional interventions, blood glucose and blood pressure control, perioperative respiratory training, minimizing nasogastric tube retention time, and optimizing perioperative blood transfusion strategies. For high-risk patients, such as the elderly, those undergoing prolonged surgeries, experiencing excessive intraoperative blood loss, undergoing total gastrectomy, or receiving open surgery, close postoperative monitoring is essential. Early recognition of pneumonia signs and timely intervention can improve patient outcomes and reduce complications. Introduction According to the Global Cancer Statistics 2018, gastric cancer is the fifth most common cancer worldwide and the third leading cause of cancer deaths [ 1 ]. Although radical gastrectomy is the only curative treatment, postoperative complications remain significant [ 2 – 7 ]. Notably, the incidence of postoperative pneumonia after radical gastrectomy ranges from 2.2% to 26% [ 8 – 13 ], leading to longer hospital stays, increased costs (up to $40,000) [ 14 , 15 ], and a mortality rate as high as 30% [ 16 , 17 ]. A previous meta-analysis on gastric endoscopic submucosal dissection identified various risk factors for postoperative pneumonia [ 18 ]. However, since radical gastrectomy remains the standard treatment for gastric cancer, a focused meta-analysis on risk factors specific to radical gastrectomy is of critical clinical significance. Research on risk factors for postoperative pneumonia following radical gastrectomy has yielded inconsistent results. For example, while some studies suggest that total gastrectomy [ 3 , 10 , 19 ] and male gender [ 7 , 20 ] are associated with a higher pneumonia risk, others do not support these associations [ 8 , 12 , 21 ]. These discrepancies likely stem from diverse study designs, where variations in patient demographics, such as some studies focused on elderly patients over the age of 75 [ 12 ], and some studies focused on patients after laparoscopic surgery [ 3 ], which may lead to differences in results and surgical settings [ 7 ], introduce heterogeneity, compounded by biases common in retrospective analyses. Statistical methods also play a role, as smaller sample sizes in some studies [ 13 ], combined with inadequate control of confounders, such as smoking or COPD, could obscure true relationships [ 21 ]. Beyond methodology, individual responses to surgical trauma differ, with some patients experiencing greater diaphragmatic impairment or immunosuppression, potentially heightening pneumonia risk [ 20 ]. Over time, technical progress and optimized preoperative care, may reduce risks, reflecting evolving surgical practice [ 22 ]. International guidelines provide practical strategies for pneumonia prevention that align with our findings. For example, the ERAS Society recommends preoperative nutritional optimization and smoking cessation [ 23 ], along with minimizing operative time and promoting early postoperative mobilization and respiratory physiotherapy [ 24 ]. Similarly, the American College of Physicians [ 25 ] and WHO emphasize preoperative risk assessments, respiratory training, and postoperative early mobilization to reduce pulmonary complications [ 26 ]. Additionally, NCCN guidelines advocate comprehensive preoperative assessments and tailored antibiotic prophylaxis for high-risk oncology patients [ 27 ], while ATS/IDSA guidelines recommend cautious antimicrobial use to prevent resistance [ 28 , 29 ]. These recommendations underscore the clinical relevance of our study by translating empirical risk factors into actionable preventive strategies. For identifying the risk factors and strength and correlations linked to pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, a thorough systematic review and meta-analysis, determined solely through multivariable logistic regression analyses to reduce the influence of confounding factors, are necessary. Such a study would provide healthcare providers with a solid scientific basis to identify populations at high risk of postoperative pneumonia and develop effective plans for symptom management. Methods This meta-analysis adhered to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [ 30 ] and was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024506161). Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria The PECOs principles (P: Participants; E: Exposures; C: Comparisons; O: Outcomes; s: Study Design) were strictly adhered to by the inclusion criteria. P: Patients (aged ≥ 18 years) undergoing radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, including both open and laparoscopic surgery. E: Multivariate logistic regression was utilized in the initial investigation to pinpoint at least one risk factor for pneumonia. C: Lack of risk factors for pneumonia. O: Any approved, globally recognized diagnostic standards or evaluation instruments for pneumonia [ 31 ]. S: Cohort and case–control studies. Exclusion criteria The entire research text couldn’t be available. Relevant information was either unavailable or inconsistent, or it could not be found by getting in touch with the original writers. The following types of studies were excluded: case studies, reviews, editorials, duplicate publications, and incomplete articles. Animal studies. Low-quality literature (NOS < 4). Search strategy From January 20, 2024, to the date of their respective inception, two reviewers independently searched the following databases: Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Chinese Periodical Full-text Database (VIP), Chinese Wan fang Data, PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus. Additionally, a backward search was carried out to find more references from the included papers and pertinent earlier reviews or meta-analyses. The reviewers combined Mesh terms with free words and appropriately used Boolean logic operators to develop search strategies. The Mesh terms and free words used included “stomach neoplasms (MeSH)”, “stomach cancer”, “gastric cancer”, “gastric neoplasms”, “radical gastrectomy”, “gastrectomy surgery”, “pneumonia (MeSH)”, “lung infection”, “pulmonary infection”, “hospital acquired pneumonia”, “aspiration pneumonia”, “risk factors (MeSH)”, “influence factors”, “predicted factors”, “relevant factors”, “dangerous factors”. The details of the utilized PubMed search approach are provided in Appendix 1. This meta-analysis only included studies published in English or Chinese. The titles and abstracts obtained from the electronic search were independently scanned by two reviewers to find possible applicable studies, which were then filtered in accordance with the inclusion criteria. Any disagreements were resolved by a third reviewer. To ensure a comprehensive literature review, we attempted to retrieve unpublished data by directly contacting the corresponding authors of eligible studies. Authors were asked to provide additional methodological details or subgroup data relevant to our analysis. Furthermore, we searched for gray literature, including conference abstracts, research proposals, and dissertations, to minimize potential publication bias. Data extraction Two experienced reviewers separately extracted the data. If there were any differences, these were worked out by consensus-building discussions or consultations with a third reviewer. Data extraction utilized a standardized Microsoft Excel spreadsheet, capturing the following details: first author, study type, publication year, total sample size, country or region, age, sex ratio, pneumonia incidence, pneumonia diagnosis, surgical procedures, and associated risk factors. Furthermore, risk factors for pneumonia were obtained from multifactorial logistic regression analysis, including odds ratio (OR), 95% confidence intervals (CI), and p -values. Quality evaluation and certainty assessment Literature quality was independently evaluated by 2 investigators. ​For cross-sectional studies, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) assessment tool was utilized, comprising 11 items ​where each item was scored as “yes”, “no”, or “unclear”. The total score ranges from 0 to 11, ​with studies categorized as: low quality (0–3), medium quality (4–7), or high quality (≥ 8) [ 32 ]. ​For case–control and cohort studies, the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) was applied, classifying studies as low (1–3), medium (4–6), or high quality (7–9) based on cumulative scores [ 33 ]. Statistical analysis The meta-analysis in this study was conducted using RevMan 5.4 software and R 4.4.2. Risk difference (RD) was selected as an indicator to evaluate the prevalence of pneumonia after radical gastrectomy, and the aggregated effect size was calculated using the general inverse variance method. Risk factors for pneumonia after radical gastrectomy were expressed using odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The OR values of the risk factors were extracted from the multivariate logistic regression analyses of the original studies, and their standard errors (SE) were calculated for meta-analysis. Meta-analyses were performed for risk factors reported in two or more studies, and descriptive analyses were performed for risk factors reported in fewer than two studies. Specifically, we extracted risk factor names, adjusted ORs, and their 95%CIs from each study and qualitatively described them in the results. Risk factors exhibiting statistical significance were categorized as high risk (OR ≥ 2), moderate risk (1 < OR < 2), or protective (OR < 1). Heterogeneity among the studies was analyzed using the Q test and I 2 statistic. An I 2 value of 0–25% indicated low heterogeneity, 26–50% indicated moderate heterogeneity, and 51–100% indicated high heterogeneity. In cases where P ≥ 0.1 and I 2 ≤ 50%, indicating no significant statistical heterogeneity among studies, a fixed-effects model was employed for the meta-analysis. Alternatively, for P < 0.1 or I 2 > 50%, which was indicative of significant heterogeneity, a random-effects model was adopted. Sensitivity analysis was carried out using the leave-one-out method and by changing the effect model. In cases of significant heterogeneity, subgroup analyses and meta-regression were conducted to explore the influence of study characteristics on the effect size. When at least 10 studies reported the prevalence rate or a particular risk factor, funnel plots were generated using R 4.4.2, and Begg's and Egger’s tests were used to assess publication bias [ 34 , 35 ]. A significance level of P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. In the presence of publication bias, the trim and fill method was applied to adjust for potential missing studies and to re-estimate the combined effect size. With a cumulative case group of 1,435 and a case–control group of 19,405, the studies’ total sample size was 20,840. Pneumonia ranged in incidence or prevalence from 2.1% to 26.38%. The research, most of which were from China ( n = 19) and Japan ( n = 8), were published between 2008 and 2023. The main methods for diagnosing pneumonia include imaging, lab work, and clinical presentation. The main features of the 27 assessed studies are shown in Table 1 . The main weaknesses in the studies rated as moderate quality were in the Outcome and Comparability domains. The Outcome domain included unclear methods for outcome assessment, no mention of follow-up time, and no reporting of follow-up results. The main issue in the Comparability domain was the lack of mention of methods to control for confounding factors (Table 2 ). These limitations may lead to inaccurate or incomplete reporting of outcome events, and the lack of control for potential confounding factors may mean that the study results are influenced by other factors, potentially introducing some bias to our overall conclusions. For example, in studies with unclear outcome assessment methods, the incidence of postoperative pneumonia might be over- or underestimated. Similarly, the lack of control for important confounding factors could mean that the associations we observed are confounded by other unmeasured factors. Due to the substantial heterogeneity observed ( I 2 = 95.8%, P < 0.001), a random-effects model was utilized to calculate the pooled prevalence. Our analysis revealed that the combined prevalence of pneumonia after radical gastrectomy was 11.0% (95% CI, 8.0%–15.0%) (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Forest plot of the prevalence of pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer Sensitivity analyses Sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of our findings, as the sequential exclusion of individual studies did not significantly alter the pooled prevalence (Fig. 3 ). This consistency underscores the reliability of the meta-analysis results, even in the presence of high heterogeneity. However, future research should address the methodological and contextual differences contributing to the observed heterogeneity. Fig. 3 Leave-one-out results Publication bias testing To evaluate potential publication bias, we initially performed a visual inspection using a funnel plot (Fig. 4 ). The plot exhibited asymmetry, indicating the possible presence of publication bias. Subsequent analysis with Egger’s test confirmed a significant small-study effect (t = 6.0095, P < 0.001), reinforcing evidence of potential publication bias (see Appendix 2). To mitigate this bias, we employed the trim-and-fill method for adjustment. The results revealed that, after imputing 11 studies, the original effect size (OR = 1.1196) decreased to OR = 1.0472, reflecting minimal change in the adjusted effect size despite the presence of publication bias. Additionally, meta-regression was employed to quantitatively assess the impact of these covariates on between-study variance (Table 4 ). With regard to surgery type, patients undergoing total gastrectomy had a prevalence of 13.64%, which was higher than the 9.90% observed in those undergoing partial gastrectomy. Similarly, the prevalence after open surgery was 13.07%, exceeding that of laparoscopic surgery. Furthermore, patients with Intraoperative blood loss ≥ 200 ml had a prevalence of 15.84%, significantly higher than the rate for those with blood loss < 200 ml. For operation duration, cases lasting ≥ 200 min showed a prevalence of 16.62%, compared to 9.93% for cases lasting < 200 min. In terms of geographical differences, the prevalence in China was 12.9%, higher than the 7.34% observed in Japan. When comparing studies by time, those conducted before 2020 reported a prevalence of 15.33%, which was considerably higher than the 7.03% reported in studies conducted post-2020. Finally, the prevalence in case–control studies was 15.40%, exceeding the 10.89% observed in cohort studies. Meta-regression was further performed to evaluate the effects of these factors, and among the variables analyzed, only the variable “Years” was statistically significant. This finding is consistent with the subgroup analysis results; however, a substantial portion of the heterogeneity remains unexplained. Risk factors for pneumonia after radical gastrectomy Among the 27 studies are multivariate analysis identified 35 risk factors in total. A risk factor was selected out and combined for the meta-analysis if it was reported in two or more studies. In the end, 16 risk factors were found for pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer were identified, and detailed information was shown in Table 5 . Forest plots of risk factors are shown in the Appendix 3. With a pooled OR of 4.58 and a 95% CI ranging from 1.84 to 11.38, diabetes mellitus was found to significantly increase the incidence of pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer ( P = 0.001). The pooled OR was determined to be 1.51, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.25 to 1.83 ( P < 0.0001). The results showed a strong correlation between the incidence of pneumonia after a radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer and the duration of the surgical procedure. Statistical testing revealed significant heterogeneity among the studies ( I 2 = 90%, P < 0.00001). The random-effects model demonstrated an independent association between perioperative blood transfusion and pneumonia following radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, with an OR of 4.21 and a 95% CI ranging from 2.51 to 7.06 ( P < 0.00001). Male gender Two studies ( n = 779) examining the association between pneumonia and male sex found statistical significance without heterogeneity, as validated by a meta-analysis [ 7 , 20 ] ( I 2 = 0%, P = 0.55). The overall OR was 3.56, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.50 to 8.42. The findings demonstrated that, after a radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, male sex was an independent prognostic factor for pneumonia. Advanced age Age-related data were extracted from eight studies involving a total of 10,760 individuals [ 12 , 13 , 19 , 21 , 43 , 45 , 47 , 51 ]. This independent meta-analysis utilized a random-effects model due to the substantial heterogeneity observed among the trials ( I 2 = 94%, P < 0.00001). The pooled OR was estimated at 1.91, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.42 to 2.58. The findings revealed a significant association between the advanced age of subjects and the incidence of pneumonia following radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer ( P < 0.0001). Nutritious status Nutritional status was evaluated in four eligible studies ( n = 3,134) [ 3 , 41 , 43 , 44 ]. The random-effects model demonstrated a significant association between nutritional status and the risk of postoperative pneumonia following radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, with a pooled OR of 2.62 and a 95% CI ranging from 1.55 to 4.44 ( P = 0.0003). Substantial heterogeneity was observed among the studies ( I 2 = 71%, P = 0.02). Total gastrectomy Relevant data were provided by three trials, totaling 4,033 individuals who had total gastrectomy [ 3 , 10 , 19 ]. For this meta-analysis, a fixed-effects model was used because there was no discernible heterogeneity between the trials ( I 2 = 0%, P = 0.91). Across the six trials, the overall OR was 2.59, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.83 to 3.66. Based on the combined data, total gastrectomy was found to be a significant independent predictor of postoperative pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer ( P < 0.0001). COPD Three studies, involving 4,402 patients who underwent radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, provided data on patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) [ 12 , 19 , 39 ]. The pooled analysis revealed that COPD was a significant risk factor for postoperative pneumonia following radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, with an OR of 4.72 and a 95% CI ranging from 3.80 to 5.86 ( P < 0.00001). The heterogeneity test did not reveal any statistically significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0%, P = 0.39). Impaired pulmonary function There were three studies [ 21 , 47 , 54 ] ( n = 1,756) that provided information on pulmonary function. Significant heterogeneity amongst the trials was found by statistical analysis ( I 2 = 92%, P < 0.00001). With an OR of 1.29 and a 95% CI spanning from 0.82 to 2.03, the random-effects model did not reveal a correlation between impaired pulmonary function and postoperative pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer ( P = 0.83). History of pulmonary disease Three separate trials totaling 2,972 participants who provided information on a history of pulmonary disease were included in this analysis [ 10 , 43 , 53 ]. The meta-analysis utilized a random-effects model because of the significant heterogeneity among the studies ( I 2 = 79%, P = 0.008). With a 95% CI spanning from 1.17 to 2.21 ( P = 0.003), the calculated pooled OR was 1.61. The results showed a significant correlation between a history of lung illness and pneumonia after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer. D2 lymphadenectomy Two studies ( n = 1,030) [ 12 , 20 ] investigating the relationship between pneumonia and D2 lymphadenectomy showed statistically significant results without heterogeneity, as confirmed by a meta-analysis ( I 2 = 0%, P = 0.73). With a 95% CI spanning from 2.29 to 7.49, the combined OR was 4.14. These results indicate that, after radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, D2 lymphadenectomy is an independent predictor of pneumonia. Hypertensive Results from two trial [ 3 , 51 ] s ( n = 1,739) examining the association between pneumonia and hypertension proved statistically significant and showed no heterogeneity. For this meta-analysis, a fixed-effects model ( I 2 = 0%, P = 1.0) was used. The combined OR was estimated to be 2.21, with a 95% CI ranging from 1.29 to 3.79. These results imply that after a radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer, hypertension is an independent predictor of pneumonia ( P = 0.004). Open operative procedure Data on the practice of open operative procedure were reported by two research [ 13 , 39 ] ( n = 7,796). A statistical analysis of the studies showed that there was a high amount of heterogeneity ( I 2 = 98%, P < 0.00001). They show that there is no association between an open surgical procedure and pneumonia after a radical gastrectomy for gastric cancer (OR = 2.81, 95% CI: 0.78 to 10.19, P = 0.11). Descriptive analysis A descriptive analysis of risk factors that could not be combined was performed in 27 studies. Preoperative comorbidities (OR = 4.008, 95 CI% = 1.768 ~ 9.086) [ 36 ], wound pain (OR = 3.428, 95 CI% = 1.557 ~ 7.548) [ 36 ], tumor located at middle third (OR = 1.86, 95 CI% = 1.14 ~ 2.64) [ 39 ], preoperative sarcopenia (OR = 5.38, 95 CI% = 1.77 ~ 16.3) [ 9 ], modified frailty index (OR = 2.72, 95 CI% = 2.02 ~ 3.31) [ 40 ], ASA classification ≥ 3 (OR = 2.202, 95 CI% = 1.398 ~ 2.866) [ 13 ], tumor diameter (OR = 1.068, 95 CI% = 1.024 ~ 1.114) [ 13 ], advanced stage (OR = 2.35, 95 CI% = 1.05 ~ 5.67) [ 3 ], time to first diet (OR = 1.175, 95 CI% = 1.06 ~ 1.302) [ 19 ], postoperative hospital stay (OR = 1.015, 95 CI% = 1.002 ~ 1.028) [ 19 ], poor performance status (OR = 17.54, 95 CI% = 3.17 ~ 97.33) [ 8 ], cardia-non-preserving gastrectomy (OR = 5.33, 95 CI% = 1.53 ~ 18.93) [ 8 ], systemic Inflammation score (OR = 2.31, 95 CI% = 1.19 ~ 4.48) [ 10 ], mechanical ventilation time (OR = 1.697, 95 CI% = 1.189 ~ 2.821) [ 43 ], preoperative use of antimicrobials (OR = 3.543, 95 CI% = 1.312 ~ 9.571) [ 45 ], excessive postoperative bed rest (OR = 2.724, 95 CI% = 1.241 ~ 5.977) [ 45 ], pathologic MMP-2 in gastric cancer (OR = 2.754, 95 CI% = 1.062 ~ 7.139) [ 45 ], pathology of gastric cancer TIMP1 (OR = 2.683, 95 CI% = 1.091 ~ 6.597) [ 45 ] and preoperative chemotherapy (OR = 2.115, 95 CI% = 1.047 ~ 4.269) [ 47 ] were the other 19 individual risk factors identified via multiple regression analysis. Our meta-analysis did not include these 19 risk factors. Sensitivity analyses Change effect model: Sensitivity analysis was conducted by applying both random-effects and fixed-effects models to assess the influence of various factors. The results revealed no significant changes in the effect sizes of individual factors, suggesting that the findings are relatively robust (Table 6 ). Leave-one-out elimination method: For studies exhibiting substantial heterogeneity ( I 2 > 50%) and involving more than two influential factors, sensitivity was further evaluated using the leave-one-out elimination method. The analysis demonstrated that heterogeneity was significantly reduced for six risk factors—prolonged postoperative nasogastric tube retention, intraoperative bleeding ≥ 200 ml, diabetes mellitus, nutritional status, impaired pulmonary function, and history of pulmonary disease—allowing the adoption of a fixed-effects model for these factors. In contrast, the heterogeneity of the remaining four risk factors showed no significant reduction, and a random-effects model was retained. Other meta-analysis results remained largely unchanged, indicating overall stability of the findings (Table 7 , Appendix 4). factors This study conducted subgroup analyses on five variables—diabetes mellitus, nutritional status, history of pulmonary disease, perioperative blood transfusion, and prolonged postoperative nasogastric tube retention—with country, surgical approach, and age as covariates. Regarding diabetes mellitus as a risk factor, country-specific differences emerged: in China, diabetes was a significant risk factor for postoperative pneumonia (OR = 2.37, p < 0.001), whereas in Japan, no significant association was observed (OR = 0.95, p = 0.90). By surgical approach, diabetes increased the risk of postoperative pneumonia in laparoscopic surgery (OR = 2.14, p = 0.02) but not in open surgery (OR = 1.89, p = 0.14). Across age groups, diabetes consistently posed a risk, with OR = 1.90 ( p = 0.007) for patients aged ≥ 60 years and OR = 1.92 ( p = 0.011) for those < 60 years. For nutritional status, malnutrition was a significant risk factor for postoperative pneumonia following radical gastrectomy in the Chinese population (OR = 2.19, p = 0.01), but not in the Japanese population (OR = 1.16, p = 0.85). Malnutrition did not significantly influence postoperative pneumonia across age groups (OR = 1.46, p = 0.211 for ≥ 60 years; OR = 1.41, p = 0.337 for < 60 years) or surgical approaches (OR = 1.53, p = 0.42 for open surgery; OR = 1.69, p = 0.20 for laparoscopic surgery), indicating it is not a consistent risk factor. Regarding history of pulmonary disease, no significant association with postoperative pneumonia was found in Chinese patients (OR = 1.34, p = 0.64), whereas it was a significant risk factor in Japanese patients (OR = 2.16, p = 0.003). The effect of pulmonary disease history was similar across age groups (OR = 1.55, p = 0.34 for ≥ 60 years; OR = 1.42, p = 0.53 for < 60 years), suggesting age does not substantially modulate this relationship. However, the risk was higher in laparoscopic surgery (OR = 2.61, p < 0.001) than in open surgery (OR = 1.62, p = 0.005), with both indicating independent risk. Further analysis of country-age interactions revealed no significant association in China across age groups (OR = 1.23, p = 0.7694), but in Japan, the elderly subgroup (≥ 60 years) showed a significant risk (OR = 2.16, p = 0.0014). Perioperative blood transfusion was a significant risk factor for postoperative pneumonia in both countries—China (OR = 3.20, p < 0.0001) and Japan (OR = 3.68, p < 0.0001)—and across surgical approaches (OR = 3.12, p < 0.0001 for open surgery; OR = 2.90, p < 0.0001 for laparoscopic surgery). This effect persisted across age groups (OR = 3.64, p < 0.001 for ≥ 60 years; OR = 4.13, p < 0.001 for < 60 years). Interaction analysis indicated a stronger effect in younger patients (< 60 years), particularly in Japan (OR = 4.61, p < 0.0001) compared to China (OR = 3.96, p < 0.0001). Due to limited studies, analysis of prolonged postoperative nasogastric tube retention was restricted to China. Prolonged retention was a risk factor for postoperative pneumonia (OR = 2.47, p < 0.0001), with a higher risk in open surgery (OR = 1.82, p = 0.02) and an independent risk in laparoscopic surgery (OR = 1.67, p < 0.001). Across age groups, prolonged retention remained a consistent risk factor (OR = 2.39, p < 0.001). The specific results are shown in Table 8 .
